content: The Misery Index is an economic indicator that was created by economist Arthur Okun. It is calculated by adding the unemployment rate to the inflation rate. The underlying assumption is that both a higher unemployment rate and worsening inflation impose significant economic and social costs on a country. There is a common misconception that the Misery Index was developed by Chicago economist Robert Barro in the 1970s. This confusion arises because Barro created a modified version of the index, known as the Barro Misery Index, which also incorporates GDP and the bank interest rate into its calculation. Some economists suggest that the components of the Misery Index—unemployment and inflation—may influence the crime rate. Research has shown a strong correlation between the Misery Index and crime rates, with the Misery Index appearing to precede changes in crime rates by approximately one year. The methods used to measure unemployment and inflation have evolved over time, which may affect the interpretation of the Misery Index. For example, data on inflation is often sourced from the U.S. Department of Labor or financial forecasting tools like the Financial Trend Forecaster®. A related metric, the Despondency Index, was developed by the Bureau of Inverse Technology. This index measures the correlation, in real time, between the suicide rate—tracked using the Suicide Box at the Golden Gate Bridge—and the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
